---
title: "Writing proofs that readers can navigate"
description: "A short guide to structure, signposting, and mathematical precision."
date: 2026-09-01
categories: [Teaching, Exposition]
---

A correct proof can still be difficult to read. Good exposition makes the logical architecture visible without diluting the mathematics.

## State the route

Before a long argument, tell the reader what the main intermediate steps will accomplish. A useful opening sentence often has the form:

> We first establish compactness, then identify every possible limit, and finally prove uniqueness.

## Separate ideas from calculations

When an estimate is long, explain its purpose before displaying it. Readers should know what the calculation is trying to prove.

## Close the loop

At the end of a proof, explicitly connect the final statement to the original claim. This is especially useful when the proof introduced several auxiliary objects.
